unverified: Yamunabai Waikar: Wikipedia calls her a leading exponent of lavani (Padma Shri 2012), but no recording of hers was found on iTunes, MusicBrainz or the lyrics archive; none is listed.
Usha Mangeshkar's Hindi 'Mungda' (Inkaar, 1977) is often called a lavani-style item song; no page read says so, so it is not used as a near.
Hindi film lavanis in general: Wikipedia's Tamasha page says some Hindi films included lavanis, but names none; none was verified.

'Nesali Pitambar Jari Ga' from Balgandharva (2011) is called 'a typical traditional Lavani' by the Times of India list, sung by Asha Khadilkar; left out because the singer credit there ('Asha Khadilkar, Bai Sundarabai') is unclear.

Sulochana Chavan's 'Mi Baya Padaliya Bhidachi' and 'Mala Hava Ga Asach' (lavanis on the archive) probably match 'Mee Baya Padliya' and 'Mala Hava Ga' on the iTunes album Mala Baghun Martoy Dola Lavnya (tracks dated 1971/1972); the match was not confirmed, so they are left out.

Sulochana Chavan's 'Tuzhya Usala Laagal Kolha' (named among her famous lavanis by Wikipedia) appears to be the refrain of 'Phad Sambhal Turyala Ga' (the archive's lyrics contain 'तुझ्या उसाला लागंल कोल्हा'); treated as the same song, not listed twice.

Film years on the Aathavanitli Gani film pages differ from Wikipedia for four films (Pinjara 1977 vs 1972, Malhari Martand 1964 vs 1965, Sawaal Majha Aika 1960 vs 1964, Rangapanchami 1960 vs 1961); Wikipedia's release dates are used.
Release years on iTunes for the Sulochana Chavan albums (1972, 1985, 1994) are digital-store dates and may not be the original LP/cassette years.
Roshan Satarkar's 'Darling Darling Kay Mhantos', Sulochana Chavan's 'Kalidar Kapuri Paan' and 'Kheltana Rang Bai Holicha', and 'Aho Jaijuichya Phula' (Shobha Gurtu, Lalita Phadke): no year found.

'Vaccines' (bamboo trumpet band) on a Courlander Music of Haiti LP: notes say it is associated with rara, but the PDF covers three volumes and which LP it is on was not checked.
Soul Jazz 'Rara in Haiti': recordist and recording year not found (iTunes artist only 'Rara Group'); the Sounds of the Universe page refused scripts (bot check).
Dominican gagá groups recorded commercially (e.g. Roldán / 'Sí Gagá' noted on a CUNY Dominican Studies page) not checked: the CUNY page returned a bot check.
Rara tech (Gardy Girault) and Lakou Mizik / Chouk Bwa Libète as modern rara-derived acts: recalled or only seen in search results, not recorded.
Boukman Eksperyans 'Konbit Zaka' original album (Libète, 1995) shown only in OCR-garbled liner text; the 1995 year used is the Rhythms of Rapture compilation's.
Release years before 1966 not found: 78 rpm and early LP son huasteco recordings (e.g. Trío Los Cantores de la Sierra, El Viejo Elpidio's earlier sides) recalled, not looked up.
Dueto/Trío Xoxocapa's founding date and members, Los Brujos de Huejutla's own studio albums: not found on a script-readable page.

Smithsonian Folkways liner notes for El ave de mi soñar (SFW40512 PDF) read, but the text layer is poor OCR, so no quote was taken from it; it names Los Cantores de la Sierra and Los Caimanes as trios Joel Monroy played in.

Huapango arribeño (Guillermo Velázquez y Los Leones de la Sierra de Xichú, El triunfo, on Tercer festival de la Huasteca, 2006) found on MusicBrainz but kept out: a separate neighbouring style with no id.
José Pablo Moncayo, Huapango (1941 orchestral piece): a classical work built on huapango themes, not added (English Wikipedia names it; no recording page was read).
Year of Miguel Aceves Mejía's original El Pastor recording: only the 1984 compilation year was found.

El Negro Marcelino y Sus Huastecos, Huasteca linda (ECO, 1973) and Los Cantores de Valles on Música huasteca (INAH/Pentagrama, 2002) found on MusicBrainz but not used: neither page ties them to son huasteco by more than a regional word.

Bihari-, Lavotta- and Csermák-era pieces whose titles do not name the genre: 'Janos Bihari Quick Hungarian' and 'Antal Csermak Palotche Hungarian' (Hungarian Gipsy Concert Music, 1992), 'Primatiális magyar (Bihari János - Lakatos Sándor feldolgozása)' and 'Magyar és friss (Lavotta János Csámpai Ivó feldolgozása)' (Déki Lakatos Sándor, Lamarti 1997), 'Lavotta Szerenad' (Mátyás Jónás, Frémeaux 2019), 'In Memory of Bihari' (100-member Budapest Gypsy Orchestra), 'Bihari János táncai' (Jánosi Együttes, on Vetettem gyöngyöt 2007): MusicBrainz shows the tracks, but no page read ties them to verbunkos by its own words (only the Bihari Wikipedia page, about the composer, not the recording).

Kalotaszeg legényes recordings (Muzsikás, Sebő Együttes, Ökrös, Halmos Béla, Csík zenekar): the scope names legényes, but no page read calls the legényes a verbunk; left out rather than tie through a general claim.

Further village and revival verbunks seen on MusicBrainz and not added to keep the list balanced: Kalamajka 'Bonchidai verbunk - Ritka Magyar' (1989), Dűvő 'Vasvári verbunk és csárdás' (1998), Ökrös Band 'Ördöngősfüzesi ritka fogásolás és verbunk' (1994), Berecz András 'Verbunk' (2011), Utolsó Óra 'Verbunk és figurázó' (1999), A Máscingók 'Keszui négyes, sűrű magyar és verbunk'. All are checkable the same way.
Sándor Lakatos (1924–1994), the best-known Budapest Gypsy band leader, is in the list only through the Frémeaux 1950s reissue; his Hungaroton LPs were not looked up.
The year of the 1950s Frémeaux recordings (Lakatos, Boross and Csenki) and of the Capella Savaria Hungaroton disc: not on the pages read, yrs left null.

Lujza Tari, 'The Verbunkos, a music genre and musical symbol of Hungary' (Bulletin of the Transilvania University of Braşov, 2012), cited on the English Csárdás page: the PDF address returns an HTML error page; not used.

Banda Espectacular Pagador / Fraternidad Morenada Central Oruro, Antología musical en bronces (2025, iTunes): seen in the search listing only; the track list was not read.

Many northern Chilean band singles of diablada 'saltos' (Banda Ecos Tocopilla, Banda Sound Machine Antofagasta, Banda La Popular Arica, Banda Wiracocha) and Puno singles: seen only in an iTunes search listing; none was read or used.
Brass Unbound (PAN Records, 1999): the page credits 'Banda Espectular Parador de Oruro / Banda Poopò'. I read this as a misspelling of Banda Espectacular Pagador, but no page confirms that.
Savia Andina, Aymuray, Sukay, Inkuyo 'Morenada de los Sapos' and other folk-group morenadas found in a MusicBrainz search: releases have no date or were not read.
Uruguayan comparsa 'Morenada' (MusicBrainz artist, Uruguay; album 'Abran cancha! Son las Lonjas del Cuareim!'): would make a near-miss for candombe, but no page read ties it to candombe.

Release years are album dates: Kjarkas 'Morenada Chacaltaya' is from the 2006 compilation 35 años, and the Diablada Azoguini anthology (2019) collects pieces dated 1998-2017 in their titles. Pagador track titles carry years (1945, 1956, 1974, 1981) that look like composition years; these were not used as recording years.

Los del Río's sevillanas of the 1970s-1980s (Sevillanas y rumbas 1972-1975 albums) and their Rocío 'Gloria': album titles seen on en.wikipedia, no track list read; only one song (from a 2019 reissue of Cantemos por sevillanas) used.

Los Romeros de la Puebla's own annual albums (1968 Sevillanas onward): discography on es.wikipedia only; the MusicBrainz artist search returned just one release (No te olvidaré, 1990) and the iTunes lookup of their 'Las mejores sevillanas' collection returned no tracks; the group is represented only by the Saura soundtrack medley.

Hermanos Reyes (Castilleja de la Cuesta), Los Giraldillos, Salmarina's own albums, Los Choqueros, Ecos del Rocío (only medley tracks titled 'Sevillanas a toda banda 1' etc. seen), Siempre Así, Raya Real, the coros rocieros (Coro de Huelva, Coro de Almonte): named as important on es.wikipedia Sevillanas, no song-level page read.
Niña de los Peines' sevillanas (es.wikipedia: first solo singer to stand out): no recording page found.
Rocío Jurado's 1962-dated 'Rocieras de Rocío' tracks: iTunes gives 1962-01-16, which is before her first records; year left open.

Viva Sevilla: es.wikipedia Sevillanas says Lorca and La Argentinita recorded sevillanas 'Viva Sevilla' in 1931, while the La Argentinita pages name 'Sevillanas del Siglo XVIII' among the 1931-32 tracks; used the latter title only.
Amigos de Gines 'El adiós' is dated 1975 by es.wikipedia (the album), the MusicBrainz release used (Sevillanas, Hispavox) is dated 1988 and is probably a compilation.
Copla singers on Sevillanas de los Cuarenta (Concha Piquer, Lola Flores, Niña de la Puebla, Estrellita Castro, Paquita Rico, Miguel de Molina): the compilation gives no recording years.
MusicBrainz answered 'busy' (HTTP 503) to several searches (María del Monte, Corraleras de Lebrija, Rocío Jurado); not retried in a loop.
